## 2

I understand why some space images might seem questionable—images can be edited, and institutions should be open to scrutiny. But the evidence for a round Earth doesn’t depend on one photograph or one space agency. Ships disappear over the horizon from the bottom up, different stars are visible at different latitudes, Earth’s shadow on the Moon during lunar eclipses is always curved, and people can circumnavigate the planet. Satellites, GPS, weather forecasting, and observations by independent scientists also rely on a spherical Earth. Taken together, these are many separate, testable lines of evidence, not one coordinated set of photographs.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it is actually made of many colors. When sunlight enters Earth’s atmosphere, it bumps into tiny molecules in the air. Blue light gets scattered in all directions more easily than colors like red and orange, so blue light reaches our eyes from across the sky.

At sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels through more air. Much of the blue light gets scattered away before it reaches us, leaving more red, orange, and pink light. That’s why the sky can look so colorful then.
